title: Transport in Plants
tagline: Water potential, the ascent of sap, phloem translocation and the loss of water by transpiration.

overview.intro: Transport in plants has no pump, so every movement in this chapter is explained by physics: diffusion, osmosis, evaporation and pressure gradients. This chapter builds the concept of water potential first, then follows water from soil to leaf through the pathway and the mechanisms that lift it, then turns to the movement of food in the phloem, and closes with transpiration and the experiments that measure it — the standard practical questions of this topic.

facts.label: Water potential
facts.value: The free energy of water per unit volume, pure water at zero, made more negative by solutes and pressure — written psi with components of solute and pressure potential.

facts.label: Pathway of water
facts.value: Soil to root hair by osmosis, then symplast or apoplast to the xylem, up the stem, across the mesophyll and out through the stomata.

facts.label: Ascent of sap
facts.value: Explained by the cohesion-tension theory: transpiration pulls a continuous, cohesive column of water upward under tension.

facts.label: Translocation
facts.value: Food moves in the phloem from source to sink along a pressure gradient, as the pressure flow or mass flow hypothesis explains.

learningOutcomes: Define water potential and predict the direction of water movement between two solutions.
Trace the pathway of water from soil to leaf, distinguishing apoplast, symplast and transmembrane routes.
Explain the ascent of sap by the cohesion-tension theory.
Describe translocation and the pressure flow hypothesis.
Set out the experiments demonstrating root pressure, transpiration and the role of stomata.

learn.title: Water potential and the movement of water

blocks.text: Water moves from where it has higher free energy to where it has lower, and water potential is the name given to that free energy per unit volume. Pure water at atmospheric pressure is given the value zero, and any addition of solute lowers it, so a solution always has a negative water potential and the more concentrated the solution the more negative the value. Pressure raises it: positive pressure such as turgor raises the potential of the water inside a cell, while tension, which is negative pressure, lowers it further. The total water potential of a solution is the sum of its solute potential and its pressure potential, and water always crosses a selectively permeable membrane from the less negative side to the more negative side — that is, from higher water potential to lower — until the two sides balance or the membrane can stretch no further. The vocabulary follows from this. A solution outside a cell that is more concentrated than the cell sap is hypertonic, and water leaves the cell by osmosis so the cell becomes flaccid and, in a plant, the protoplast pulls away from the wall in plasmolysis. A solution less concentrated than the cell sap is hypotonic, water enters and the cell becomes turgid as the wall resists further entry and the pressure potential rises until entry stops. An isotonic solution produces no net movement, and the cell is said to be incipiently plasmolysed. Solute potential depends only on how many dissolved particles there are, so a sugar solution and a salt solution of the same molarity differ because one dissociates. Pressure potential is what makes plant life possible: the turgor of cells holds leaves and soft tissue rigid, drives the opening of stomatal guard cells, and provides the force of cell expansion during growth — without it a plant wilts long before any water is lost from the symplast itself. In the soil, water is held by adhesion to particle surfaces and by capillarity, and the plant must extract it against that hold, which is why a plant wilts in soil that is still visibly damp.

items: Water potential is the free energy of water per unit volume; pure water is zero.
Solute lowers water potential, making it negative; more solute means more negative.
Pressure raises water potential; tension lowers it.
Total potential is solute potential plus pressure potential.
Water crosses a membrane from higher to lower water potential — that is, less negative to more negative.
Hypotonic makes a cell turgid, hypertonic makes it flaccid and plasmolysed, isotonic gives no net change.
Turgor pressure holds soft plant tissue rigid and drives guard cell opening.
Soil water is held by adhesion and capillarity, so the plant must extract it against that hold.

items.note: The cells lose water to an atmosphere drier than their sap, turgor falls and the soft tissues can no longer hold the stem upright.
The salt solution outside is hypertonic, so water leaves the animal’s cells and it collapses — osmosis working against a soft-bodied animal.

learn.title: The pathway of water and the ascent of sap

blocks.text: Water enters the root through the epidermis, and the root hairs increase the absorbing surface enormously by increasing it. From the epidermis it must cross the cortex to reach the xylem, and it can do this in three ways. The apoplastic route moves water cell to cell through the cellulose walls and the intercellular spaces without ever crossing a membrane, which is fast but uncontrolled; the symplastic route crosses from cytoplasm to cytoplasm through the plasmodesmata that connect neighbouring cells, which is slower but selective; and the transmembrane route crosses each cell membrane in turn, entering and leaving the vacuole. All three converge at the endodermis, because the Casparian strip of suberin in its walls blocks the apoplastic route and forces every molecule to cross a membrane — this is the checkpoint at which the plant controls what enters the vascular cylinder. From the endodermis the water crosses the pericycle and enters the xylem, where it is under tension and at low water potential, so the gradient favours its entry. The ascent through the stem is explained by the cohesion-tension theory. Transpiration at the leaf surface removes water from the mesophyll cells, which lowers their water potential so they take water from the xylem, and this raises the tension on the column of water in the xylem vessels. Water molecules cohere strongly to one another by hydrogen bonding, and they adhere to the lignified walls as well, so the column does not break under tension but transmits the pull downward to the root; the entire path from mesophyll to root hair therefore remains under tension with a continuous gradient of decreasing water potential, and water is pulled up in a steady stream. The pull can lift water hundreds of metres, far more than root pressure alone could manage, which is why root pressure — the positive pressure generated when the root actively loads salts into the xylem — matters only in short plants, in the spring before leaves open, and at night when transpiration stops. Root pressure shows itself as guttation, the droplets exuded from the hydathodes at leaf margins in a damp morning, and as the bleeding of a cut stump.

items: Water enters by root hairs and crosses the epidermis.
Three routes through the cortex: apoplastic through walls, symplastic through plasmodesmata, transmembrane across membranes.
The Casparian strip blocks the apoplast and forces selective crossing at the endodermis.
Water enters the xylem down a gradient of water potential.
Transpiration lowers the water potential of mesophyll cells so they draw from the xylem.
Cohesion between water molecules and adhesion to walls keep the column continuous under tension.
The tension is transmitted to the root, pulling water up as a stream — the cohesion-tension theory.
Root pressure lifts water only in small plants, in spring and at night.
Guttation and stump bleeding are visible evidence of root pressure.

learn.title: Translocation in the phloem and transpiration

blocks.text: Food moves in the phloem, and unlike the ascent of sap it is a living process that can be stopped by killing the tissue. The accepted explanation is the pressure flow or mass flow hypothesis: loading occurs at the source, where sucrose is actively transported into the sieve tubes at the leaf, lowering their solute potential so water enters from the adjacent xylem by osmosis and the hydrostatic pressure rises. That high pressure at the source, combined with unloading at the sink — a growing root, a fruit or a storage organ, where sucrose is actively removed and water follows back to the xylem — sets up a pressure gradient along which the solution flows en masse from source to sink. The companion cells supply the energy and control the sieve tube elements, which are alive but enucleate, and the sieve plates allow the bulk flow through while the cytoplasm streams along. Several observations support the theory: the sap of the phloem is concentrated and under pressure, translocation is fastest in the direction of mass flow and is stopped by cooling, which halts the loading, or by killing the tissue — unlike water in the xylem, which continues to rise in a dead stem for a while. Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from the aerial parts, and it is the engine of the whole water path. About ninety-nine per cent of the water absorbed is lost by transpiration, most of it through the stomata and a little through the cuticle as cuticular transpiration. The stoma is a pore between two kidney-shaped guard cells, and its opening depends on the water potential of those cells: when light falls, guard cells take up potassium ions and chloride, their solute potential falls, water enters by osmosis, the cells become turgid and, because their inner walls are thicker than the outer ones, they bow apart and the pore opens; in the dark the solutes leave, water follows, the cells go flaccid and the pore closes. The rate of transpiration depends on environmental conditions — it rises with light, warmth, low humidity, wind and a larger leaf surface, and falls in dry air — and the plant must balance the carbon dioxide it needs against the water it loses, which is the central trade-off of life on land. Several forces oppose that loss and keep water in the xylem: cuticle and wax reduce cuticular loss, sunken stomata and hairs trap moist air at the leaf surface, rolled leaves and reduced leaf area cut loss in xerophytes, and a thick cuticle with sunken stomata in a cactus reduces loss to almost nothing. Experiments to know are the potometer, which measures uptake as a proxy for loss, the cobalt chloride paper test and the greased leaf experiment, which separate stomatal from cuticular loss, and the permanent slide of a leaf showing stomatal distribution on the two surfaces.

Sucrose is actively loaded at the source, water follows by osmosis and pressure rises.

Translocation stops when the tissue is killed or cooled; the xylem flow does not.
Transpiration is the loss of water vapour, mostly through the stomata.
Guard cells open the pore by taking up solutes and becoming turgid, and close by losing them.
The rate rises with light, warmth, wind and dry air and falls with humidity.
Cuticle, hairs, sunken stomata, rolled and reduced leaves all limit water loss.
A potometer measures uptake as a measure of transpiration.

blocks.text: Every practical in this topic is an application of the same physical ideas, so they can be handled as a set rather than learned one by one. The potometer measures the rate at which a leafy shoot takes up water, which is used as a measure of transpiration because the water lost and the water taken up are nearly equal over a short period. The shoot is cut under water so no air enters the xylem, the apparatus is sealed, and the position of the bubble is marked over a fixed time; the volume drawn up per minute gives the rate. Variations change one variable at a time — the lamp distance for light, a beaker of water over the shoot to raise humidity, a fan for wind — and the comparison between runs gives the effect of each. The rheotropism-free control matters here: the shoot must be left to equilibrate first, because the initial uptake includes water that the cut surface absorbs. The cobalt chloride paper test separates stomatal from cuticular loss: the blue paper turns pink as it absorbs water vapour, and it does so much faster in a area covered on the lower surface than where both surfaces are sealed with grease, which locates the stomata and shows that most loss passes through them. A permanent preparation of a leaf epidermis, stained and viewed under the microscope, shows the same thing directly — the number of stomata on the two surfaces can be counted and compared, and bulliform cells can be seen in a grass leaf. Osmosis is demonstrated with a membrane bag of sugar solution in water, which gains weight and may burst the bag as water enters, and with a potato osmoscope, a potato cube hollowed out, filled with sugar solution and weighed: the rise in the level and the increase in mass show water entering down the potential gradient. Plasmolysis and deplasmolysis are observed under the microscope by running a strong salt solution under a coverslip and then replacing it with water, watching the protoplast pull away and then return. Root pressure is shown by a cut stump bleeding, or by a detopped plant in a manometer. What each experiment needs is the same discipline as the theory: state the apparatus, describe what is varied, record what is observed, and only then draw the conclusion — the examiner marks the logic of the sequence, not the apparatus list.

items: The potometer measures uptake as a proxy for transpiration and needs an airtight, cut-under-water set-up.
One variable at a time: light distance, humidity, wind, each compared against the same control.
Cobalt chloride paper turns pink faster where stomata are exposed, locating the loss.
An epidermal peel under the microscope counts stomata on the two surfaces directly.
A membrane bag of sugar solution gains weight in water, demonstrating osmosis.
A potato osmoscope shows water entering and raising the sugar solution level.
Plasmolysis and deplasmolysis are followed by replacing salt solution with water under the coverslip.
Every answer states apparatus, variable, observation and conclusion in that order.

questions.prompt: Define water potential and state what a solute does to it.
questions.answer: Water potential is the free energy of water per unit volume, or the tendency of water to move, and it is measured in units of pressure. Pure water at atmospheric pressure is taken as the reference value of zero, so every other state is expressed relative to that. Adding a solute lowers the free energy of the water because the solute particles attract water molecules and restrict their movement, so the solute potential is negative and the total water potential of the solution falls below zero; the more solute present, the more negative the value. Pressure works in the opposite direction, raising the potential, so the total potential of a cell is the sum of its solute and pressure potentials. Water always moves across a membrane from higher, less negative potential to lower, more negative potential until the two sides are equal.
questions.explanation: Definition, the zero reference, the effect of solute and of pressure, and the direction of movement.

questions.prompt: Explain how a stoma opens and closes.
questions.answer: Each stomatal pore lies between two kidney-shaped guard cells whose walls are unevenly thickened, being thicker on the side facing the pore. When light falls on the leaf, the guard cells begin to take up potassium ions and chloride from the surrounding cells, and they also convert stored starch to sugar, so their solute potential falls. Water then enters the guard cells by osmosis from the neighbouring epidermal cells because the water potential inside is now lower. The cells become turgid and, because the outer wall of each cell is more extensible than the thicker inner wall, the cells bow apart and the pore between them opens. In the dark, or when the plant is short of water, the solutes and sugars leave the guard cells, water follows by osmosis, the cells lose turgor and become flaccid, they collapse towards one another and the pore closes. The opening is therefore a consequence of turgor change driven by solute movement, which is why light, carbon dioxide concentration and water supply all affect stomatal opening.
questions.explanation: Solute entry, water following, turgor and the differential wall thickness for opening; the reverse for closing.

questions.prompt: State three environmental factors that increase the rate of transpiration.
questions.answer: Light intensity increases transpiration because the stomata open in the light for photosynthesis, and the greater radiation also warms the leaf. Temperature increases the rate because the water molecules have more kinetic energy, so they evaporate from the mesophyll surfaces faster and the gradient between the leaf interior and the air steepens. Wind increases the rate by sweeping away the saturated layer of vapour that clings to the leaf surface, so the gradient between the leaf and the surrounding air remains steep and evaporation continues. Low humidity of the surrounding air has the same effect, since dry air can accept much more vapour before becoming saturated.
questions.explanation: Any three with the mechanism — stomatal opening, kinetic energy, removal of the saturated layer, or humidity.

questions.prompt: Explain the cohesion-tension theory of the ascent of sap and state why root pressure cannot account for the movement in a tall tree.
questions.answer: The cohesion-tension theory explains how water rises in the xylem against gravity without any pump at the top. Transpiration removes water vapour through the stomata, and because the mesophyll cells are in contact with a thin film of water, their water potential falls as the vapour is lost. They therefore take water from the adjacent xylem vessels by osmosis, which lowers the water potential of the xylem further and increases the tension on the water column it contains. Water molecules cohere strongly to one another through hydrogen bonding, so they form a continuous, unbroken column through the vessels and tracheids, and they also adhere to the lignified walls of those elements, which helps resist the breaking of the column. The tension developed at the leaf is transmitted along this cohesive column all the way to the root, so the whole path is under negative pressure and water is pulled upward from the soil to replace what has evaporated. The system behaves like a rope being pulled from the top rather than pushed from below, and the pull can raise water hundreds of metres. Root pressure cannot do this work because it is a positive pressure generated only by the active loading of ions into the xylem of the root, and it can generate only about one atmosphere of force — enough to lift water a few metres at most, as in a small plant or a sapling. In a tall tree the tension generated by transpiration is negative and can be many times greater in effect than root pressure, and root pressure is in any case absent during the day, when transpiration and the demand for water are greatest. Root pressure is therefore visible only in minor phenomena such as guttation at night and bleeding from a cut stump, while the ascent of sap in a mature tree depends entirely on the pull from the leaves.
questions.explanation: Tension generated at the leaf, cohesion and adhesion maintaining the column, transmission of tension to the root, then the explicit comparison with root pressure and its limited magnitude and timing.

questions.prompt: Describe how the pressure flow hypothesis explains translocation in the phloem, and give the evidence that supports it.
questions.answer: The pressure flow hypothesis explains the movement of sucrose from where it is made to where it is used or stored, in terms of a hydrostatic pressure gradient between the two. At the source, usually a mature photosynthesising leaf, sucrose is actively loaded into the sieve tubes of the phloem against a concentration gradient, using energy supplied by the companion cells. The sucrose concentration inside the sieve tube rises sharply, so its solute potential falls, and water is drawn in from the adjacent xylem by osmosis. The influx of water raises the hydrostatic pressure inside the sieve tube at the source. At the sink — a growing root, a developing fruit or a storage organ — sucrose is actively removed into the surrounding cells for use in respiration or conversion to starch, which raises the solute potential of the sieve tube, so water leaves by osmosis and returns to the xylem, lowering its hydrostatic pressure. The result is a pressure gradient from the high-pressure source to the low-pressure sink, and the whole column of sieve sap flows en masse down that gradient, carrying sucrose with it. Several observations support the mechanism. The sap of the phloem is a concentrated solution under pressure, as measurements with a pressure bomb show. Translocation is bidirectional, which matches source and sink positions that vary — downward in a leafy stem, upward to a developing fruit in spring. It is stopped by cooling, which halts the energy-requiring loading, and by killing the tissue, since the sieve tubes must be alive for loading and unloading to occur; by contrast, water continues to rise in a killed stem for some time because the xylem mechanism is physical. And metabolic inhibitors that block loading reduce translocation while leaving the water flow intact, which separates the two systems cleanly.
questions.explanation: The four steps of loading, water entry, flow and unloading, then the evidence set: pressure, direction, sensitivity to cooling and killing, and inhibitor evidence.

questions.prompt: A plant is kept in a closed humid chamber with its leaf surface lightly greased, leaving only the stomata ungreased, and the weight loss is measured. Explain what the set-up tests and predict the result if the chamber is then illuminated.
questions.answer: The set-up is designed to separate the two routes by which a leaf loses water. Greasing the leaf surface seals the cuticular route, so any water now lost must depart through the stomatal pores, and weighing the plant measures transpiration as a direct loss of mass. In the dark or unilluminated condition, the stomata are partly closed because the guard cells have not taken up solutes, so the rate of weight loss is low and steady — this gives the baseline of cuticular plus minimal stomatal loss. When the chamber is illuminated, the guard cells of the ungreased stomata take up potassium and chloride, their water potential falls, water enters by osmosis, the cells become turgid and the pores open. Carbon dioxide now enters for photosynthesis and water vapour escapes far more freely, so the rate of weight loss rises measurably within minutes — the slope of the mass-against-time graph steepens. The comparison therefore demonstrates two things: that stomata are the principal route of water loss, since the greased areas losing cuticular water contribute little, and that light controls stomatal opening, since illumination alone changes the rate with no other variable altered. A further control — greasing a leaf completely, or using a leaf whose stomata are on one surface only — would confirm that the effect is stomatal rather than a change in cuticular permeability caused by warming under the light.
questions.explanation: What the grease controls, the baseline, the predicted opening on illumination and the steepening rate, with the conclusion and control noted.
